report:
## Conclusion: Regular Vitamin C intake does **not** prevent colds for most people

The evidence is consistent and well-established: taking vitamin C regularly does **not** reduce your chances of catching a cold in the general population. The most authoritative source on this is the **Cochrane review** (Hemilä & Chalker, 2013), which pooled 29 trials involving over 11,300 participants and found a pooled risk ratio of 0.97 — essentially no meaningful effect on cold incidence for ordinary people.

However, there are two important nuances:

1. **It may slightly shorten cold duration.** Regular supplementation of at least 200 mg/day was associated with reducing cold duration by about **8% in adults and 14% in children**. A 2023 meta-analysis in *BMC Public Health* also found vitamin C reduces the severity of cold symptoms.

2. **One exception exists.** People under extreme physical stress — such as marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in subarctic conditions — saw roughly a **50% reduction in cold risk** with regular vitamin C intake, according to the Cochrane review.

Harvard Health, the Mayo Clinic, and the Cochrane review all agree on the bottom line: vitamin C won't stop you from getting a cold, but it may make colds slightly shorter and less severe. It remains an essential nutrient for overall immune function, wound healing, and collagen formation.

### Sources
- Cochrane Review: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold
- Harvard Health: https://www.health.harvard.edu/diet-and-nutrition/myths-and-truths-about-vitamin-c
- BMC Public Health meta-analysis (2023): https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-023-17229-8
- Mayo Clinic: https://newsnetwork.mayoclinic.org/discussion/mayo-clinic-minute-can-vitamin-c-keep-the-common-cold-away/
